title: Gradient Descent
description: See how gradient descent walks downhill on a loss landscape, why it zig-zags, and how momentum and Adam fix it. Free and interactive.
youWillLearn: What the gradient is: the direction of steepest uphill
Why every step goes against the gradient
How the learning rate decides between crawling, zig-zagging and blowing up
What momentum and Adam change, and when they help

story.title: Find the bottom, blindfolded
story.body: Imagine standing on a hillside in thick fog. You want to reach the lowest point, but you can only feel the ground under your feet. The map shows the landscape from above: green is low, lavender is high. The white ball is you.
story.keyIdea: Training a model is exactly this: the landscape is the **loss**, and the lowest point is the best model.

story.title: Feel the slope
story.body: Even in fog you can tell which way the ground tilts. That tilt, measured in both directions, is the **gradient**. It points straight uphill, so the red arrow points the other way: downhill.
story.keyIdea: The gradient tells you which way is up. Go the opposite way.
story.math: For a height `f(x, y)` the gradient is `(∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y)`. Here `f = 0.5·x² + 5·y²`, so the gradient is `(x, 10·y)`.

story.title: One step downhill
story.body: Take a step against the slope. How far? The **learning rate** times the steepness: steep ground means a big step, flat ground a small one. Then stop, feel the slope again, and repeat.
story.keyIdea: One update = new position = old position − learning rate × gradient.
story.math: `x ← x − lr · ∂f/∂x` and `y ← y − lr · ∂f/∂y`, with `lr = 0.18` here.

story.title: Why it zig-zags
story.body: This landscape is a **ravine**: the walls are steep but the floor slopes gently. The steep walls produce big steps that overshoot to the other wall, while the gentle floor produces tiny steps forward. So the ball bounces from side to side and creeps along. The chart shows the height dropping fast, then slowly.
story.keyIdea: Plain gradient descent struggles when the landscape is much steeper one way than the other.

story.title: Step size is everything
story.body: A smaller learning rate stops the bouncing but crawls along the floor. A bigger one bounces higher and higher: on this ravine, anything above about **0.2** makes every step overshoot more than the last, and the ball flies off the map.
story.keyIdea: Too small is slow. Too big explodes. The right size depends on the landscape.
story.math: Across the ravine the slope is `10·y`, so each step multiplies `y` by `1 − 10·lr`. Above `lr = 0.2` that factor is bigger than 1 in size, and `y` grows.

story.title: It got there, slowly
story.body: After 40 steps the ball reaches the bottom. Two famous upgrades make this faster. **Momentum** remembers the last steps, so the side-to-side bounces cancel out and the forward motion adds up. **Adam** scales each direction by how steep it usually is, so every direction gets a sensible step. Try them in the Lab with *Compare all three*.
story.keyIdea: Almost every neural network is trained with gradient descent, usually with momentum or Adam.

sections.heading: What is gradient descent?
sections.body:
Gradient descent is the method almost every machine learning model uses to learn. You write down a **loss**: one number that says how wrong the model is. Then you repeatedly nudge the model's numbers in the direction that lowers the loss fastest. That direction is the negative of the **gradient**.

In lesson 1 the landscape had two directions (slope and height of a line). A neural network has millions, but the idea is the same: feel the slope, take a small step downhill, repeat.

sections.heading: The learning rate
sections.body:
The learning rate decides how far each step goes. Too small and training takes forever. Too large and each step jumps over the bottom, possibly landing higher than where it started; then training **diverges**. The best value depends on how steep the landscape is, which is why it is usually tuned by trying a few values.

On a landscape that is much steeper in one direction than another (a *ravine*), no single learning rate is good for both directions. That is what the zig-zag in this lesson shows.

sections.heading: Momentum and Adam
sections.body:
**Momentum** keeps a running velocity: each step adds the new gradient to most of the previous velocity. Bounces that change sign cancel out; steady pushes in one direction build up speed. It also helps roll through small bumps and shallow valleys.

**Adam** keeps two running averages: one of the gradient (like momentum) and one of its squared size. Dividing the first by the square root of the second gives every direction a step of similar size, whether that direction is steep or flat. It is the default choice for training most deep networks.

rows: Zig-zags in ravines; stuck in shallow valleys
Can overshoot and circle the bottom
Can stop short of the very bottom

sections.heading: Valleys and saddles
sections.body:
Real loss landscapes have more than one valley. Gradient descent only knows the ground under its feet, so it settles in whichever valley it rolls into first, which may not be the deepest (*Two valleys* in the Lab).

A **saddle** is a point that is a minimum one way and a maximum the other way, like a horse saddle. The slope there is zero, so a ball balanced exactly on it would stay. A tiny nudge sends it off downhill (*Saddle* in the Lab). In big networks, saddles are far more common than bad valleys.

faq.a: The gradient points in the direction where the height increases fastest. We want the height (the loss) to decrease, so we step the opposite way.

faq.q: How do I pick a learning rate?
faq.a: Try a few values spaced by about ×3 (0.001, 0.003, 0.01, …) and keep the largest that still makes the loss go down steadily. If the loss jumps around or grows, it is too big.

faq.q: Does gradient descent always find the best answer?
faq.a: Only when the landscape has a single valley, like the bowl and the ravine here (and the loss in lesson 1). With several valleys it finds a good one, not necessarily the best.

With lots of data, computing the exact slope uses every example and is slow. Stochastic gradient descent estimates the slope from a small random batch of examples each step. The path gets noisier, but each step is much cheaper.
No. Adam is a great default, but plain gradient descent with momentum sometimes generalises better and is still used to train many image models.

byHand.problem: Find the w that makes the loss `L(w) = (w − {target})²` as small as possible without solving it directly: start at `w = {w0}` and take {steps} gradient-descent steps with learning rate `η = {lr}`.

steps.title: Differentiate
steps.body: The gradient says which way is uphill. At `w = {w0}` it is negative, so the loss goes down when w grows.

steps.title: Take the first step
steps.body: Move against the gradient, scaled by the learning rate: `w₁ = {w1}`.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.body: Apply the same rule from each new w. Every row starts where the previous one ended: `w₂ = {w2}`, `w₃ = {w3}`.

steps.title: Watch it converge
steps.body: With this learning rate the distance to {target} halves at every step, and the loss falls to {lossEnd}. More steps would bring w as close to {target} as we like.

byHand.answer: After {steps} steps `w = {w3}`, only {gap} away from the true minimum at `w = {target}`.
byHand.labNote: The Lab's Paper landscape is this same loss, started at `w = {w0}` with `η = {lr}`. Step through it: the ball lands on {w1}, {w2} and {w3}, the numbers in your table.
